To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
weak and strong convergence are different and that the weak error of the wave equation is twice the order of strong convergence.
the weak error for the wave equation is proportional to the square root of the stepsize, and that for the linearized CHC equation the weak error is of order 1.5.

for linear evolution equations with additive Gaussian noise: (1) weak and strong error converge at the same rate; (2) the error is dominated by the time discretization, and (3) higher order time discretization schemes are beneficial if the solution is less regular
In summary, our research is concerned with
the weak error of numerical approximations of linear evolution equations driven either by additive Gaussian noise or by a linear multiplicative Gaussian noise.
the weak error analysis of numerical schemes for the wave equation and the linear Cahn-Hilliards equation.

the weak error analysis of fully discrete approximations of linear evolution equations driven either by additive Gaussian white noise or by a linear combination of additive and multiplicative noise terms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the error of the fully discrete scheme is of the order $\sqrt{\triangle t}$ in the $L^2$-norm and of order $\triangle t^{\frac{1}{2}}$ in the $H^{-1}$-norm.
the weak convergence rate for fully discrete schemes is the same as that of the corresponding continuous time scheme.
the weak order is twice the strong order.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the weak error analysis of fully discrete schemes is more challenging than that of continuous in time schemes and that weak convergence of order 1/2 is possible for linear parabolic equations with additive Gaussian noise.
, for the wave equation, we have a rate of weak convergence that is twice the rate of strong convergence and for the heat equation we have a rate that is the same as the strong rate.
, for linear equations, we have a complete picture of the weak error for both the parabolic and hyperbolic cases.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in contrast to parabolic equations, for hyperbolic equations the weak error is dominated by the strong error and hence the weak error can be analyzed via standard techniques.

the error in the numerical approximation of stochastic integrals can be analyzed separately from the error in the approximation of the evolution operator, which allows one to use the standard error estimates for finite element approximations and the theory of stochastic integration.
the theory of weak convergence is a very powerful tool for analyzing the convergence properties of numerical schemes for linear evolution PDEs driven by additive noise.
